items.stem: What must be agreed before any exploitation activity begins in a penetration test?

options.text: Rules of engagement defining scope, timing and authorised techniques
options.rationale: Correct: rules of engagement and authorisation bound the test and keep it legal.

options.text: The names of all of the client's customers
options.rationale: Not required and would be a privacy concern.

options.text: A promise to find at least one critical finding
options.rationale: Outcomes cannot be promised in advance.

items.explanation: Correct: rules of engagement and authorisation bound the test and keep it legal.

items.stem: Which two items make a penetration-test finding genuinely actionable? (Select TWO)

options.text: Reproducible steps or evidence that demonstrate the issue
options.rationale: Correct: reproducibility lets the team confirm and fix the issue.
Correct: remediation guidance turns a finding into action.

options.text: The exact timestamp the tester had lunch
A screenshot of the tester's desktop wallpaper
options.rationale: Provides no evidence of the vulnerability.

items.explanation: Correct: reproducibility lets the team confirm and fix the issue.; Correct: remediation guidance turns a finding into action.

items.stem: Why is gaining an initial foothold usually not the end of a realistic engagement?

options.text: Because attackers typically escalate privileges and move laterally to reach real targets
options.rationale: Correct: post-exploitation and lateral movement show the true business impact.

options.text: Because the first host is always worthless
options.rationale: The first host may matter; the point is impact goes further.

options.text: Because tools stop working after the first host
options.rationale: Tools do not stop after initial access.

options.text: Because the test must always run for exactly 30 days
options.rationale: Duration is set by the engagement, not a fixed rule.

items.explanation: Correct: post-exploitation and lateral movement show the true business impact.
